As a life long IT/Computer professional, the data needs to be split up, not residing in a single location. This is the opposite of the overall trend in computing.

E.g. (1) Each centralized computer had it's own telephone/communications network. Now we have the Internet. (2) Each disk based data storage was managed by different, disparate software systems. Now we have DBMS, (3) We used to have separate telephone, cable TV, over the air TV channels, rented physical movie VCR tapes/DVD disks, now it all arrives over the single Internet connection to our home. (4) We used to have multiple computer vendors with their own, unique hardware and operating systems, now we have standard hardware and Windows or a Unix/Linux variant.

Data centers are the continuation of the trend. But consolidation also creates single points of failure. It is easier to manage and operate, and easier to disrupt.

(I started when computers were HUGE, and I was a teenager, in the late 1960s. I saw the hardware infrastructure of the predecessor of the Internet in the 1970s. It has been a ride!)

My estimate of "Entrenched" all-item PCE inflation as of June is 3.34%, down from 3.52% for May.  This calls for a Fed Funds rate target of 4.51% to 5.14%, depending on how aggressively the Fed chooses to achieve its 2% target.  The current rate of 3.64% is at least 87 bp too low.  

This estimate is based on a univariate Recursive Least Squares model with AR(1) transients and a best-fitting average lag of 21.6 months.  It uses the Cleveland Fed's month-end Nowcast of the June PCE-PI for timeliness.  Year over year PCE inflation (using the Nowcast for June) is 3.80%, but that has an average lag of only 6 months, far too short a perspective.   Tomorrow's June CPI announcement will slightly change the June PCE Nowcast, but not enough to substantially change the entrenched inflation estimate.  

The Taylor Rule uses the Fed's 2.0% target with a natural real rate of 0.5% and either 150% or 200% feedback from entrenched inflation to the Funds rate, and sets aside unemployment.  The current rate was about right  when it was set last December, but entrenched inflation has crept up since then.
